## The Treaty Mechanism

| Component | Value | Source |
|:----------|------:|:------|
| Global military spending | $2.72T/year | SIPRI 2024 |
| Treaty redirect | {{< var treaty_reduction_pct >}} | Policy parameter |
| Annual funding unlocked | {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}} | = military x 1% |
| Bond payouts (10%) | $2.72B/year | Incentive Alignment Bonds |
| Political allocation (10%) | $2.72B/year | Campaign infrastructure |
| **Net R&D budget** | **{{< var dih_treasury_to_medical_research_annual >}}** | = $27.2B - $2.72B - $2.72B |
| Campaign cost (one-time) | {{< var treaty_campaign_total_cost >}} | $250M viral + $650M lobbying + $100M reserve |
| Annual benefits (peace + R&D) | {{< var treaty_peace_plus_rd_annual_benefits >}} | Peace dividend + trial cost savings |

## Calculation Chain

The logic builds in six steps.

**Step 1: The Backlog**

| Input | Value | Source |
|:------|------:|:------|
| Diseases without effective treatment | {{< var diseases_without_effective_treatment >}} | Orphanet 2024 (95% of ~7,000 rare diseases) |
| Current discovery rate | {{< var new_disease_first_treatments_per_year >}} | FDA + ODA historical data |
| Backlog clearance time | {{< var status_quo_queue_clearance_years >}} | = 6,650 / 15 |

**Step 2: Trial Capacity Multiplier**

| Input | Value | Source |
|:------|------:|:------|
| Pragmatic trial cost/patient | {{< var dfda_pragmatic_trial_cost_per_patient >}} | 10x conservative vs. $97 meta-analysis median (Ramsberg & Platt 2018, 108 trials) |
| Traditional Phase III cost/patient | {{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient >}} | FDA study median |
| Annual R&D budget | {{< var dih_treasury_to_medical_research_annual >}} | From treaty mechanism above |
| Fundable patients/year | {{< var dih_patients_fundable_annually >}} | = budget / cost per patient |
| Current trial slots | {{< var current_trial_slots_available >}} | Global enrollment |
| **Capacity multiplier** | **{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier >}}** | = fundable / current slots |
| Accelerated clearance time | {{< var dfda_queue_clearance_years >}} | = 443 / 12.3 |

**Step 3: Timeline Shift**

| Component | Value | Derivation |
|:----------|------:|:-----------|
| Discovery acceleration | {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_treatment_acceleration_years >}} | = (443/2) x (1 - 1/12.3) |
| Efficacy lag elimination | {{< var efficacy_lag_years >}} | Post-Phase I access removes Phase II/III delay |
| **Total timeline shift** | **{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_years >}}** | = discovery + efficacy lag |

**Step 4: Health Impact**

| Input | Value | Source |
|:------|------:|:------|
| Global annual DALY burden | {{< var global_annual_daly_burden >}} | WHO/IHME GBD 2021 |
| Eventually avoidable fraction | {{< var eventually_avoidable_daly_pct >}} | Conservative estimate (see below) |
| Timeline shift | {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_years >}} | Step 3 |
| **DALYs averted** | **{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_dalys >}}** | = burden x avoidable% x shift |

**Step 5: Cost-Effectiveness (Two Framings)**

| Framing | Cost | DALYs | Cost/DALY |
|:--------|-----:|------:|----------:|
| Treaty campaign | {{< var treaty_campaign_total_cost >}} | {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_dalys >}} | {{< var treaty_cost_per_daly_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag >}} |
| Direct funding (NPV at {{< var npv_discount_rate_standard >}}) | {{< var dfda_direct_funding_queue_clearance_npv >}} | {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_dalys >}} | {{< var dfda_direct_funding_cost_per_daly >}} |

Note: Costs are discounted at {{< var npv_discount_rate_standard >}} social discount rate; DALYs are undiscounted (standard in GBD methodology).

**Step 6: Risk Adjustment**

| Input | Value | Derivation |
|:------|------:|:-----------|
| Political success probability | {{< var political_success_probability >}} | Conservative (99% failure assumed) |
| Risk-adjusted cost/DALY | {{< var treaty_expected_cost_per_daly >}} | = $0.0018 / 1% |
| Risk-adjusted vs. bed nets | {{< var treaty_expected_vs_bed_nets_multiplier >}} better | Still superior at 1% success |

## Key Assumptions Requiring Sign-Off

::: {.callout-warning}
## 1. Eventually Avoidable Fraction: {{< var eventually_avoidable_death_pct >}} of disease deaths
Single most influential assumption. Remaining ~7.4% covers accidents, violence, and fundamentally irreducible causes.

**Our defense:** {{< var unexplored_ratio >}} of the therapeutic search space remains untested ({{< var safe_compounds_count >}} safe compounds x {{< var trial_relevant_diseases_count >}} diseases = {{< var drug_disease_combinations_possible >}} pairings, only {{< var exploration_ratio >}} tested). {{< var drug_repurposing_success_rate >}} of approved drugs gain new indications, demonstrating effective treatments exist but haven't been matched to conditions. Life expectancy rose from ~47 to ~79 since 1900, with most gains from preventing deaths once considered inevitable. At 50%, all headline numbers halve but cost-effectiveness remains strong.

**Question:** Is {{< var eventually_avoidable_death_pct >}} defensible, or what figure would you use?
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 2. Trial Capacity = Discovery Rate (Linear Assumption)
A {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier >}} increase in trial slots produces a proportional increase in the discovery rate ({{< var new_disease_first_treatments_per_year >}} -> {{< var dfda_first_treatments_per_year >}}).

**Our defense:** Linear is conservative. {{< var valley_of_death_attrition_pct >}} of promising compounds are abandoned at the "valley of death" because Phase II/III costs ({{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient >}}/patient) make them uneconomical, not because they lack efficacy. Eliminating this cost barrier would reactivate ~{{< var additional_drugs_from_cost_elimination >}} additional approvals. Knowledge accumulation creates potential for *superlinear* returns: each trial generates efficacy signals, biomarker insights, and combination data that inform subsequent trials. Pre-1962 decentralized physician-led testing achieved drug development at {{< var pre_1962_drug_development_cost_2024_usd >}}/drug vs. today's {{< var pharma_drug_development_cost_current >}}, consistent with trial throughput being the binding constraint.

**Question:** Should we model diminishing returns, or does the superlinear case justify the linear assumption as a middle ground?
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 3. Political Success Probability: {{< var political_success_probability >}}
Risk-adjusted at {{< var political_success_probability >}} (99% failure), cost-effectiveness ({{< var treaty_expected_cost_per_daly >}}/DALY) still beats bed nets ({{< var bed_nets_cost_per_daly >}}/DALY).

**Our defense:** Ottawa Treaty (landmines, 1997) negotiated in under two years via 1,000+ NGO coalition. Montreal Protocol achieved near-universal ratification. The 1% Treaty adds Incentive Alignment Bonds tying legislators' career incentives to treaty support, a mechanism neither precedent had.

**Question:** Is {{< var political_success_probability >}} the right baseline? What probability breaks even with bed nets?
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 4. $1B Campaign -> $27.2B/yr Government Funding (Treaty Leverage)
{{< var treaty_vs_direct_funding_leverage >}} leverage assumes {{< var treaty_campaign_total_cost >}} advocacy campaign redirects {{< var treaty_reduction_pct >}} of global military spending.

**Our defense:** We present both framings: treaty ({{< var treaty_cost_per_daly_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag >}}/DALY, cost to funder) and direct funding ({{< var dfda_direct_funding_cost_per_daly >}}/DALY, cost to society). For foundations, the treaty framing is relevant: $1B unlocking $27.2B/yr in government spending is standard policy advocacy leverage.

**Question:** Which denominator should we lead with for foundations?
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 5. Pragmatic Trial Cost: {{< var dfda_pragmatic_trial_cost_per_patient >}}/patient
Deliberately conservative.

**Our defense:** Ramsberg & Platt (2018) reviewed 108 embedded pragmatic trials across multiple therapeutic areas; of 64 with cost data, **median was $97/patient**. Our central estimate is **10x higher than the meta-analysis median**. RECOVERY achieved {{< var recovery_trial_cost_per_patient >}}/patient across 186 sites. Cost reductions come from structural factors: existing healthcare encounters, EHR-based data capture, broader eligibility. At our upper CI bound ($3,000/patient), the capacity multiplier drops from 12.3x to ~3.8x, still cutting the backlog from 443 years to ~116 years.

**Question:** Is the meta-analysis median ($97) or our conservative anchor ({{< var dfda_pragmatic_trial_cost_per_patient >}}) more appropriate?
:::

**Note on framing:** All health impact figures are cumulative over the acceleration window, not annual. This is inherent to the model: treatments arrive X years earlier than an unknown future discovery date, and the benefit is the disease burden during that gap. Same methodology as smallpox eradication ROI calculations.
